I shall confess at the outset that I hold very little patience for these modern telephone contraptions, and my exchange with the young man at the broadband company's helpline did nothing to improve my opinion of the matter; I was transferred four times, made to repeat my account number on each occasion, and left on hold to a recording of what I can only describe as saxophone music for the better part of forty minutes. I mention this only so that what follows may be properly appreciated. Having given up entirely on the telephone, I asked my grandson, Oliver, to simply 'have a look' at the router himself when he called round on Sunday. He was finished, by the clock on my mantel, in under four minutes, without once dialling a single number or raising his voice to anyone. When I asked how on earth he had managed what an entire call centre could not, he showed me a small screen on his own telephone displaying what he called a 'diagnostic,' as though the router itself had simply told him, in its own language, precisely what was the matter with it. I sat down rather heavily in my armchair afterward. Sixty years I have lived alongside telephones, wirelesses, and now these little glowing boxes in every room, and I confess I had never once considered that a machine might report its own ailments the way a patient describes symptoms to a doctor. Oliver seemed to find my astonishment rather funny. I have been turning the whole business over in my mind ever since, and I still cannot quite settle on what to make of it.

Every few years someone publishes a tidy chart claiming the vowels of a certain valley town have shifted a full step in one generation, and every few years I find myself squinting at their sample size. This synthesis works through eleven such generational comparisons from small communities, and frankly only four hold up once you account for how the recordings were elicited — reading a word list into a microphone is not the same as ordering coffee. What survives the cull is a modest but real drift in how young speakers round a handful of back vowels, nothing like the dramatic reinventions the headlines promised.

Our six-person field team departed from the trailhead at what our itinerary rather optimistically described as 0600 hours, though in practice we did not actually assemble all six pieces of camping equipment, seventeen sample bags, two working GPS units, and Marguerite's inexplicably heavy cast-iron skillet into the two support vehicles until closer to 0740, a delay that set the tone, frankly, for the entire eleven-day expedition into the upper canyon system. The first three days were consumed almost entirely by logistics of a kind that will be tediously familiar to anyone who has organized a remote survey: negotiating access with two separate ranching families whose land bordered the access road, replacing a blown tire on the supply truck using a jack that turned out to be rated for a substantially lighter vehicle, and waiting out an unseasonal two-day rainstorm inside a canvas mess tent that, despite everyone's best efforts at reinforcement, leaked steadily onto the exact corner where we had unwisely stored the reference maps. Evenings were spent, as they always are on these trips, debating the relative merits of instant versus 'real' coffee, a debate I will not relitigate here except to say that Desmond's instant-coffee advocacy remains, in my considered opinion, indefensible. It was not until day six that conditions allowed us to reach the target exposure, where we spent a single, intensely productive afternoon measuring strike and dip across the exposed fault scarp and collecting oriented samples from six discrete vein-fill generations, finding that the youngest calcite veins cut consistently across the older quartz-filled fractures at a steep, unrelated angle, indicating at least two distinct episodes of fracture reactivation separated by a substantial interval of quiescence. The remaining five days of the expedition were, in the interest of full disclosure, spent almost entirely on the return hike, which took considerably longer than planned owing to a washed-out section of trail and Marguerite's insistence, vindicated in the end, on carrying the skillet the entire way rather than caching it as the rest of us had suggested.

Our onboarding process for new engineers has historically taken about a week and a half longer than it should, mostly due to accumulated undocumented steps that only live in senior engineers' memory, so this quarter I took it upon myself to write a proper onboarding runbook and, more importantly, automate as much of it as possible rather than just describing it in prose that nobody reads past the first paragraph. Most of the runbook covers account provisioning, VPN setup, and access requests to three internal systems that each have their own approval workflow with different SLAs, which has been the single biggest source of delay historically and is largely out of engineering's control to fix. The one piece that was actually within my control was repository setup, and I've now got that down to a single onboarding script that clones the four repos a new hire needs, configures the upstream remote tracking branches correctly so pull and push default to the right places without extra flags, and installs a pre-commit hook that runs the linter before every commit rather than relying on CI to catch formatting issues after the fact, which was generating an embarrassing number of red builds from people who genuinely didn't know the style rules yet. The only snag left is that the hook installer copies the script directly into the repository's internal hooks folder, which means it silently vanishes the moment someone clones the repo fresh, since that folder isn't tracked as part of the repository content itself. I'd like the hook to survive a fresh clone without every new hire needing a separate manual install step, is a tracked hooks directory with a one-time hooksPath configuration entry the standard fix, or is there a cleaner convention for this now?

So GridWorks pushed an update over the weekend, and true to tradition, the changelog was three lines of corporate poetry about 'enhanced performance' that told me precisely nothing useful. I spent Monday morning doing my usual ritual of poking at every menu to see what actually changed, because apparently that's my job now. The new dark mode is fine, I guess — slightly less blue than the old one, which nobody asked for but also nobody's mad about. The keyboard shortcut for freezing panes moved, which cost me about four minutes of confused clicking before I found it again, a real inconvenience worth exactly one eye-roll. The autocomplete for function names is marginally snappier, which I appreciate in the same way I appreciate a slightly faster elevator. Here's the part that actually matters, buried under all that: the pivot table's 'sum by category' aggregation is now silently excluding any row where the category cell has trailing whitespace, which describes roughly a third of our imported CSV data because our CRM export has always had that quirk, and it always used to sum fine before this update. state.question: What's the right spacing between rows when planting carrot seeds?
state.answer: Carrots are one of those vegetables people either love growing or give up on entirely after a bad first attempt, and there's not much middle ground from what I've seen over the years. Soil prep matters more for carrots than almost anything else in the garden, since rocky or compacted soil causes the roots to fork or twist rather than growing straight down. A broadfork or a deep tilling pass before planting makes a noticeable difference in root shape come harvest. Germination is also notoriously slow and uneven compared to other root vegetables, often taking two to three weeks before you see consistent sprouting, which trips up a lot of first-time growers who assume nothing took and till the bed back under. Keeping the top layer of soil consistently damp during that stretch, without waterlogging it, is the single biggest factor in getting an even stand. Carrot rows should sit about 12 inches apart, with seedlings thinned to roughly 2 inches apart within the row once they've sprouted. Thinning is the step most people skip out of reluctance to pull up seedlings, but crowded carrots end up small and misshapen, competing for root space underground even when the tops look fine above the surface.

Let's talk about my shop, because apparently that's the part everyone wants to hear about. I've got a track saw that cost more than my first car, a dust collector with enough suction to reorganize the neighbor's recycling bin, and a benchtop planer I researched for two months before buying. My Instagram followers, all four of them, seem very impressed.

What they don't see is me standing in the garage for twenty minutes trying to remember which way the grain runs before I make a cut, or the pile of 'practice' pocket-hole joints in the scrap bin that are there because my first five attempts split the wood. Last weekend's project was a simple picture ledge, the kind of thing that's basically two boards and a strip of trim, and I still managed to route the rabbet on the wrong edge and have to start the board over.

I watched about six tutorials before I even touched the saw, and I'm still checking a reference chart taped to the wall to remember the difference between a dado and a rabbet, which apparently is a very basic thing to mix up if the comments on my last post are anything to go by. The fancy track saw did make the cut dead straight, I'll give it that, credit where it's due. But straight cuts don't help much when you're not totally sure yet how the joint is supposed to go together in the first place. I'm getting there, slowly, one slightly-too-short board at a time. At least the shop looks professional, even if the guy running it very much is not.

state.question: How often should the filter in the Everdry dehumidifier be cleaned?
state.passage: I have owned my Everdry dehumidifier for some three years now, and I have found it to be a reliable companion in the damp cellar. The manual that accompanied it, printed in a pleasingly large typeface, instructs the owner to remove and rinse the filter every thirty days under lukewarm water, and to allow it to dry fully before it is replaced. One is also advised to empty the collection bucket daily during the wetter months, though I confess I sometimes forget until it is rather too full.

state.question: What does the Blue Comb newt primarily eat?
state.passage: I first came across a Blue Comb newt years ago while helping my niece with a school project on pond life, and what stuck with me was how the guidebook described its diet, mostly small aquatic insects, mosquito larvae, and the occasional water flea, all snapped up along the muddy margins of slow streams. We spent an entire afternoon at the creek behind her house trying to spot one eating, though we only ever saw it sitting still on a submerged log. Apparently they'll also take tiny snails when insects are scarce, according to the same guidebook.

So I bought this dress for my cousin's wedding back in April — different wedding, long story, we have a lot of them in my family — and it's a gorgeous color in person, exactly like the swatch, but I noticed after about an hour of wear that the zipper on the side kept sliding down on its own no matter how I adjusted it, which was mortifying at the reception when my aunt had to help me fix it in the bathroom twice.

I want to give a full account of this order because I think future buyers deserve the complete picture. I purchased three items together — a wool coat, a pair of gloves, and a scarf — all part of the same checkout and, according to the confirmation email, all sent in a single box via the seller's preferred carrier. The gloves and scarf arrived within the promised four-day window, neatly packaged in tissue paper, and both are lovely; no complaints there whatsoever. The coat, however, was apparently separated from the rest of the shipment at some point, because it never appeared in that first box at all. When I contacted support, they informed me that the carrier's manifest showed the coat as a separate parcel that had, in their words, 'gone missing in the network,' and that a trace request would take five to seven business days to resolve. Two weeks passed with no updates, so I called again, and only then did the seller agree to send a replacement coat at no additional charge, this time via a different carrier entirely. That replacement arrived six days later in perfect condition. In total, from the original order date to finally having the complete set of three items in hand, twenty-six days elapsed, twenty-two of which were spent waiting on a coat that had simply vanished somewhere between the warehouse and my house. I want to stress that the garments themselves, once I actually had them, were exactly as described and beautifully made. My frustration is entirely with how long it took, and how little visibility I had, to get the missing piece sorted out.

Let me walk through the timeline in full, since I think it's relevant context: the order confirmation quoted an estimate of five business days, which felt reasonable for a paperback shipped domestically, and for the first four days the tracking updated normally, moving through two intermediate facilities as expected. On day five, however, the tracking simply stopped, no scans, no updates, nothing, and it stayed frozen in that state for an additional eleven days before a single new scan appeared showing the book had, for reasons never explained, been routed to a center in a different state entirely before finally correcting course and reaching my mailbox sixteen days after the original estimate.

So the kids have been begging to watch this rocket launch for like two weeks now because their science teacher did this whole unit on it and they're both convinced they're going to grow up to be astronauts which is adorable but also means I've had to answer approximately four hundred questions about fuel tanks, and the launch is supposedly happening Saturday morning except every single forecast I've checked says there's a decent chance of thunderstorms rolling through right around the scheduled window, and apparently if the upper level winds are too strong they'll have to scrub it entirely and push to the backup date sometime the following week, which would be a nightmare because that's the same weekend as my niece's birthday party and I really don't want to be driving two hours each way twice in one weekend, so right now I'm just refreshing the weather radar every hour like that's going to change anything, packing snacks and blankets just in case we do go, and trying to explain to a seven year old why a rocket that's sitting right there on the launch pad, fully fueled and ready, might not actually go anywhere if there's too much wind way up in the atmosphere that we can't even see from the ground, which honestly doesn't make a ton of sense to a kid but that's rocketry for you, everything has to line up perfectly or the whole thing just waits, sometimes for days, and we won't know for sure until a few hours before whether we're actually driving out there or staying home and watching it on a livestream instead, if it goes at all this weekend.
